Where it began

Imran Tahir was born in Lahore on 27 March 1979 and learned his cricket there. As the eldest child he went out to work at 16, selling in a shopping mall to help his family, until trials earned him a place in Pakistan's Under-19 side. He went on to tour with Pakistan A.

The next step up did not come in Pakistan, so he tried county cricket in England and then settled in South Africa, a country that had long been short of good spinners. He became a resident there in 2005, aged 26, and spent several hard years in domestic cricket before he qualified to play for his new country in 2011.

The player

He arrived in international cricket in a hurry. In his first one-day match, at the 2011 World Cup in Delhi, he took four wickets, and he picked up 14 in the five games he played at that tournament. His Test debut followed against Australia at Cape Town later in 2011.

He played 20 Tests for South Africa between 2011 and 2015 and took 57 wickets at 40.25. His best day came in Dubai in October 2013, when his first five-wicket haul in Tests, 5 for 32, helped South Africa beat Pakistan by an innings and level the series. He took eight wickets in that match.

What made him special

His stock ball was the googly, and he bowled it with the joy of a man who had waited a long time for his chance. In the shorter game he became one of the best in the world: in 2017 he sat at the top of the rankings for bowlers in both one-day and Twenty20 internationals, he was the first South African to take seven wickets in a one-day international, and his four wickets against Sri Lanka in 2015 helped South Africa win a World Cup knockout match for the first time.

The bat was more of a passenger. He made 130 Test runs at 9.29, though nine not-outs show he could hang around when asked.

Away from the middle

Few cricketers have packed so many bags. He played for eight English counties, a record, and for teams in India, the Caribbean and well beyond. He won the purple cap as the leading wicket-taker for the Chennai Super Kings in 2019, and in 2023 he captained the Guyana Amazon Warriors to their first Caribbean Premier League title. In 2019, aged 40, he became the oldest South African to play in a World Cup match, and he bowled the very first over of that tournament.

And finally

Every wicket set off a celebration known as The Marathon: a joyful run away across the field. Batsmen who got out to him at least had the comfort of knowing someone was enjoying it.
